notes:
Six report defects, all found by auditing a live airline site and checking
every claim against the page.

**Counted sentences are spelled correctly.** A report could say "1 internal
link carrys UTM parameters". The helper that agrees a verb with its count was
handed only the count, so it could not spell "carries" — five findings printed
a misspelled verb at exactly one, which is the most common count in a real
audit. The helper now takes the verb.

**Advice no longer names a trade you are not.** Business markup typed
"Organization" was told to change to "Plumber, Dentist, Restaurant, Attorney".
Those are examples written for one kind of customer and shown to every
customer, and following them publishes a false claim about your organisation
to a search engine. The advice now points at schema.org's own list.

**The worst finding in the report says which domain.** A page canonicalising
to another site is CRITICAL and on its own takes a report to F. It named the
page and not the destination — so you were told something catastrophic was
happening and left to go and find out what. It now names the domain, and says
when that domain carries your own name.

**Two findings about one job say so.** Pages that build their content in
JavaScript were reported twice — once as invisible to AI crawlers, once as
delivering no content in the initial HTML — with the same page list and the
same remedy, and the plan billed two jobs. It is one job and now reads as one.

**A 404 is no longer reported as a bot filter.** URLs that answered "page not
found" were described as a rate limiter or an edge rule, with advice to open
them in a browser and find out which. The server had already answered. The
finding now says so and points at the broken-link and sitemap findings, which
own the real work.

**Redirect chains name the URL you have to change.** The finding listed the
destination — which redirects nowhere — while its own advice asked you to
change the first URL in the chain. It now lists the URL that redirects, and
the example no longer drops the destination on long chains.
